#28054. Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2782 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying a fresh computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense.
  • While it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16, with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price.
  • Before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying a fresh computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense. Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia’s new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models.

While it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16, with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you’re looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error.

Before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia’s pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn’t skimp on the specs.

Recent findings suggest that asus has released numerous ProArt laptops, but this one is notable for including the new Nvidia Spark RTX chip in its most powerful configuration. The Spark N1X has a 20-core Grace CPU, divided between 10 high-performance Arm Cortex-X925 cores and 10 power-efficient Arm Cortex-A725 cores. The performance cluster reaches boost speeds between 4.0 and 4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores peak at 2.8 GHz. Memory caching on the processor totals 49MB, split between 24MB of shared L3 cache and 25MB of L2 cache.

Graphics and AI are the purview of the Nvidia GB20B Blackwell GPU. It packs 6,144 cores in this configuration across 48 streaming multiprocessors, backed by its own 24MB L2 cache. These 5th-generation Tensor Cores support the full suite of Nvidia technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, and NVFP4. In all, you’re looking at up to 31 TFLOPS of FP32 graphical performance and about 1,000 TOPS of FP4 AI compute.

Sources indicate that asus will sell this device in two memory configurations (plus some lower-specced retailer-specific SKUs), but the one I’ve been testing (and the one that makes the most sense alongside the RTX Spark) has 128GB of LPDDR5x RAM. It supports up to 300GB/s of raw bandwidth, which is fast for shared system memory. However, using a dedicated GPU typically gets you higher throughput with a GDDR7 memory interface. Still, you get several times more memory than a gaming GPU in this machine.

This is essentially an Nvidia Spark DGX workstation with a screen and keyboard. It also runs Windows 11, which lowers the barrier to entry if you want local AI agents. While many local AI setups focus on 27-billion-parameter models that will fit on a video card, the Asus ProArt P16 can easily load models with 100-plus billion parameters, with enough left over for lighter background AI tasks.

Industry observers note that nvidia and Asus say the Spark’s AI compute and ample memory are enough power to run frontier-level AI models locally. That means you can get powerful AI compute without running through your allotment of expensive tokens or sending all your data to a server in the cloud. Ignoring the AI angle, the ProArt P16 has to be a good laptop before it makes sense for even the most AI-obsessed buyers to consider it. Luckily, it gets all the basic laptop things right.

It’s nice to see a wide array of ports on this machine. There are three USB-C ports with USB4 support, and they’re split between the left and right sides. That makes connecting devices and charging much easier. There’s also a legacy USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 port, full HDMI, a 3.5 mm jack, and an SD card reader.

The machine comes with a beefy 140 W USB-C charger, which can get you a few hours of use in just a minute or two of charging. Asus says you can get up to 12 hours of use per charge, but that depends very much on what you’re doing. Watching video at low brightness might get you even more than 12 hours, but expect somewhat less for mixed use and even less for heavy AI workloads. In my (unscientific) testing, after a full workday and tinkering with AI on the side, the P16 usually has about 30 percent of its battery left.

Industry observers note that the 16-inch 120Hz OLED display is overall very good, sporting a 4K+ resolution of 3840 x 2400. The stacked (tandem) pixels mean you get an incredibly high 1,600 nits of peak brightness. However, tandem OLEDs do tend to look a bit grainy with solid colors at lower brightness levels. I’ve laid eyes on two P16 units, one of which was noticeably more grainy than the other—so that’s something to look out for. However, the texture is easy to ignore at normal viewing distances and mid-to-high brightness.

In a recent development, the trackpad is enormous (150.3 x 99.5 mm) and relies on haptic clicks instead of a physical mechanism. This is a relatively new thing for Windows laptops, which are still catching up to Apple’s trackpads. That mentioned, the ProArt’s pad works very well. It’s appropriately sensitive, and you can adjust the click intensity and detection threshold.

The keyboard is a little on the narrow side for a larger laptop, but the keys feel great. There’s ample travel, the tactility is sharp, and the firm keyboard deck ensures no flex at the bottom of each keystroke. The aluminum chassis is overall very solid, but it only comes in white or black, with the latter being your only option for the high-end model. The matte case looks great, but it is a magnet for smudges (particularly the plastic of the keys).

In a recent development, unlike previous ProArt laptops that had standard GPUs, there’s no dedicated memory for the RTX Spark’s graphics and AI cores. Windows sees the machine as having 64GB of system RAM and 64GB of video memory, but in reality, this shared 128GB of memory is adjusted dynamically based on what you’re doing.

Industry observers note that since this is a Windows machine, there is some overhead that limits your AI workloads. On a DGX Spark box with the same underlying hardware, all the memory is available for AI. Here, you’re capped at about 110GB. That’s still a huge amount of memory for AI, far surpassing what you can get on even the most expensive consumer-level GPUs.

There are a few clear advantages to making the ProArt P16 your AI hub. Running an AI model locally on the Spark’s Blackwell cores lets you keep all your data private. When you interact with ChatGPT or Gemini, your interactions and data become training and advertising fodder. You’re also trusting the AI provider to run your workloads on the right model, and they’ll often route requests to cheaper ones to save money.

Industry observers note that with an RTX Spark laptop, you have total control over how the AI operates. That also means you have to do all the setup and management yourself. The ProArt comes with a few Asus apps, which will streamline setup for a subset of AI-powered tasks, but installing a third-party agent is where things get interesting (but not always good).

Nvidia’s laptop AI chip is optimized for desktop clients like OpenClaw and Hermes, allowing you to download the AI models of your choice in a fairly simple graphical UI. I tested various models in different size ranges. Asus recommends starting with Qwen 27B, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that splits the difference between size and efficiency. I also loaded a few versions of Google’s Gemma open models in the same size range.

According to recent reports, but these are all small enough that you could run them on a high-end GPU. To push the Spark, I grabbed a few larger models like the Qwen Flash Next, a 90GB download with 125 billion parameters. This model occupies almost all the shared memory when active, whereas the smaller ones won’t even go beyond the GPU’s reserved 64GB.

Sources indicate that the nice (and scary) thing about setting up a local agent on Windows is that it can control the PC. Once the model is loaded in your preferred AI framework, you can just ask it to handle additional configuration. Need to set up access for your online accounts? Just ask. Manage installed tools and apps? Just ask. Surely nothing could go wrong, right?

In a recent development, in short order, I set up agent workflows to access and analyze data from test email accounts, manage local files, enhancement a coding project, and analyze the content of images in my photo library. I also used ComfyUI workflows to generate images and videos locally without worrying about running through a limited allotment of tokens in the cloud. I’ll admit, I don’t have much use for media generation, but some of these local image models have gotten surprisingly good. Of course, the machine itself is expensive enough that you could pay for the most extravagant AI aims for a few years before breaking even. Still, the data and compute are all yours.

In a recent development, A few tragic tales about local agents nuking file directories or exposing data have made the rounds, and that’s a real concern when you start giving these things access to your PC—these models can do whatever you can do while sitting at the keyboard. I tested the P16’s AI capabilities with that in mind, ensuring I had no irreplaceable or sensitive data on the machine. Agents are supposed to seek authorization before taking action, but mistakes may happen, even if you’re being careful.

The agents didn’t make any huge mistakes in my testing, but watching the chain of thought bounce around can be maddening, like an unguided robot vacuum bouncing into walls. But like a vacuum, today’s AI agents usually get to the right place.

Sometimes, it does feel very futuristic. You give the machine a problem or tell it to troubleshoot something, and it does it without sharing any data with anyone. It’s a different way of using a PC. That’s cool, but it’s also not without frustration. Even though these models are often able to arrive at the correct result, they may not do so very swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that during normal operation, the Asus ProArt P16 is whisper-quiet. As soon as you start running inference for AI, though, the fans kick into high gear. The machine absolutely burns through the enormous 100 Wh battery, which is the largest cell you can legally bring on an airplane in the US. You really only get about two hours of inference without the power cable, and you might not get as much done as you’d think in that time. For example, scanning a day’s emails and generating action items takes around five minutes with a mid-weight model.

Recent findings suggest that with simple tasks, models like Qwen 27B can churn through 20 or so tokens per second (with default “medium” effort mode). That’s a bit slower than you’ll get with cloud-based frontier models, which are also more capable thanks to their powerful server hardware. As long as you don’t need to ask it if Taiwan is a country, Qwen seems like the best option for local AI currently. Google’s mid-weight Gemma models can occasionally hit up to 40 tokens per second, but that figure tends to come down to a quarter of that speed for more complex tasks.

It has been revealed that while Qwen Flash Next does produce better results, it takes so long I usually stick with the smaller models—it chugs along at just a few tokens per second unless you drop its thinking level. You can still make use of all that RAM by running multiple concurrent agents, though. That may be the real promise of RTX Spark machines, but that requires you to have a lot of AI-powered projects in mind. If you’re just using a Spark laptop as an alternative to keeping a ChatGPT window open, you should probably pay for ChatGPT Pro instead of buying a $7,000 PC.

While the RTX Spark is aimed at AI workloads, it’s also an all-around speedy Windows platform. It is, however, an Arm-based chip with 20 Nvidia Grace CPU cores. Microsoft has a sordid history with Windows on Arm, but things are finally in a better place.

The Windows Prism emulator can run x86 and x64 programs well enough that you won’t usually notice the difference, and some past software gaps, like Google Drive and VPN apps, have been addressed with native Arm versions. So you don’t need to fear Arm chips on Windows anymore unless you have very specific legacy software and hardware needs.

It has been revealed that in daily use, the ProArt P16 with RTX Spark is extremely responsive. It’s still usable even when you fill up the memory with AI agents running inference in the background. There are very few systems that directly compare to the RTX Spark right now, but here are some system benchmarks of the Asus ProArt P16.

Nvidia has pushed the idea that Spark can be your primary gaming machine, too. But here, emulation is more of a bother. There are virtually no native Arm games for Windows, and emulation takes a bite out of your performance. Titles that require system-level anti-cheat measures may not run because those cannot be emulated. However, Nvidia has made progress here, collaborating with some major vendors like Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, and Denuvo to support their technology on Spark. It’s still early, though, and you may encounter errors.

The GPU component of the Spark N1X is equivalent to the most powerful Blackwell-based gaming GPUs on the market, but emulation means performance won’t quite measure up. You also have to remember that the ProArt P16 has an incredibly high-resolution OLED screen. Running games at native resolution, even without the emulation overhead, is already pushing the limits of the hardware.

It has been revealed that aside from the benchmark numbers, I put the ProArt P16 to work playing some games. While they ran well enough to play, it’s not as simple as cranking the settings to max like you would on an x86 system with a Blackwell GPU. For example, Baldur’s Gate 3 is not exactly a graphical tour de force, and it’s more CPU-bound than some other AAA games.

I had to make some compromises to maintain 60 fps, even in less busy areas of the game. It was basically a trade-off between lowering detail and using aggressive DLSS or dropping the game below native resolution. You can expect Spark-based machines like this to run most games with high graphical settings, but ultra settings will be out of reach if you want to maintain good frame rates.

Sources indicate that in a purely technical way, it’s cool that you can run powerful 100GB AI models on a laptop. Devices like the DGX Spark and DIY GPU clusters can perform similar tasks, but having everything centralized on one machine makes it more appealing as a way to get things done with AI, and Windows makes it easy to get started.

The ProArt P16 can be your one and only computer, handling gaming, productivity, and AI inference. However, it can be hard to really take advantage of all the AI capabilities of the machine. You’re looking at running either one or two large, powerful agents at very slow speeds or a collection of smaller models much faster. That means you need to have plenty of AI applications in mind. Otherwise, you might as well get a standard laptop.

You probably already know if that’s something you want. The kind of person running multiple concurrent agentic tasks using cloud systems might benefit from a PC like the ProArt P16, and in some extreme instances, they might want to spend $7,000 on the machine with 128GB of RAM. However, you could also step down to the 64GB model to save a few thousand dollars and still get some useful AI capabilities as models get more efficient.

According to recent reports, the Asus ProArt P16 is really a niche machine. If you want something primarily for gaming, an x86 system with a discrete GPU makes more sense, and a lighter, productivity-focused laptop is better for most buyers. The ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of how a local AI-powered future could work, but it’s not a good purchase for anyone but the most fervent AI boosters right now.

We put 7 rugged tablets in our lab sauna – here’s how they performed at 106°F

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ZDNET’s lab in Louisville, KY, has come up with some pretty creative ways to test devices, such as using a silicon ear to test earbuds or recreating a living room with different floor types to test robot vacuums.
  • Also: We tested 7 rugged tablets – these 2 outlasted the cold and heat best.
  • Industry observers note that our latest test examined seven of the best rugged tablets from Samsung, Oukitel, Dell, Getac, and DT Research and how well they handled heat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ZDNET’s lab in Louisville, KY, has come up with some pretty creative ways to test devices, such as using a silicon ear to test earbuds or recreating a living room with different floor types to test robot vacuums.

Also: We tested 7 rugged tablets – these 2 outlasted the cold and heat best.

Industry observers note that our latest test examined seven of the best rugged tablets from Samsung, Oukitel, Dell, Getac, and DT Research and how well they handled heat. Gianmarco Chumbe, our product testing manager, built a dry sauna for the tablets that mimics a very hot day (up to 106°F) to see which tablet lasted the longest under the extreme conditions.

It turns out Chumbe has experience building this kind of thing. “I’m a reptile keeper, and I don’t like paying for luxury enclosures, so I build them myself,” he stated. “When I set out to replicate a hot environment holding around 105°F, to simulate what users might experience on a very hot worksite, I realized it was a very similar setup to what I’d already been building at home.”.

Chumbe built a 40 × 20 × 20-inch enclosure with walls made of half-inch PVC board and a quarter-inch acrylic front panel to view the tablets during testing. A 400 Watt fan-forced PTC heater sat at one end of the chamber, while a 20 × 12-in aluminum baffle, positioned 10 inches in front of the heater, blocked its direct airflow, so no tablet was directly heated by it. Most importantly, a circulation fan ran continuously to keep the air evenly mixed.

Sources indicate that “The only difference is that reptiles need a temperature gradient, from a hot side to a slightly cooler one, whereas [for tablets] we needed a constant temperature spread evenly across the whole rig. We solved that by building in proper air mixing,” he remarked. Also, the tablets’ sauna didn’t include any form of moisture.

According to recent reports, the thermostat was consistently set between 104 and 106°F, with the heater cycling every 2 minutes (30 seconds on and 90 seconds off). A second, independent thermostat cut power to the heater if the air reached 115°F, protecting the units if the main thermostat failed. Finally, a single 1 ⅛-in. port, sealed around the cables, carried the power and sensor cords.

Also: How we test products and service at ZDNET.

In a recent development, testing began after placing the seven tablets on a raised rack inside the sauna. Each tablet started at 100% battery, with Airplane Mode on, and the screens were set to 500 nits of brightness (or the closest equivalent). Chumbe ran a looped playback of the same 1080p H.264 video file (no audio track) in VLC, with the system audio muted on each of the tablets.

To document battery degradation, a lightweight Python script ran on each tablet throughout the test and logged the battery level every minute until the tablets shut down or entered a dormant state at 1% battery life.

It has been revealed that lastly, even though these tablets could certainly operate in hotter temperatures, we capped out the sauna at 106°F since the rig was designed to operate unattended. Higher temperatures increase the risk of batteries overheating, and thus fire hazard.

Out of the seven tablets we tested in the sauna, the Oukitel RT10 lasted the longest at 32.07 hours. However, that wasn’t the tablet Chumbe found most impressive in the tablet sauna.

In a recent development, “What surprised me most was how resilient the Samsung Galaxy Active 5 Pro was. Even after sitting at 1% battery for hours, it still let me use all of its features, including saving, editing, and uploading test data,” Chumbe noted. “It’s a small unit compared to the others, but it holds its ground remarkably well.”.

Industry observers note that also: Want the best Wi-Fi laptop? We tested 7 models – here’s what our lab found.

Recent findings suggest that the Samsung Galaxy Active 5 Pro lasted 15.20 hours in the tablet sauna, outperforming other more expensive rugged models like the Getac F120 and the  DT Research Rugged Tablet DT312RP. The Active 5 Pro’s 10,100mAh battery came in second place (lasting 22.88 hours) in our baseline room-temperature testing, and first place in our cold test, lasting 12.47 hours at -6°F.

While you may not be able to build your own tablet sauna at home, our lab’s test results show how rugged tablets can withstand extreme conditions for those who need to use one while camping/hiking, out in the field, or on a construction site on a hot summer day.

The Oukitel RT10 and the Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 5 Pro are both solid picks for rugged tablets that can withstand the heat (or a tablet sauna).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals.
  • Sources indicate that the reinstatement, declared Monday morning, is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr.
  • That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals.

Sources indicate that the reinstatement, declared Monday morning, is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures.

Recent findings suggest that huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the manufacturer, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

It has been revealed that president Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Organization, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”.

Appearing on CNBC Monday morning, Trump mentioned that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said.

In a recent development, “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump noted. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.”.

In a recent development, huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the manufacturer’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak.

Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement.

Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board noted it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back.

Sources indicate that in Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation.

In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The organization has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a upcoming chief compliance officer.

This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.
  • SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).
  • Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.

“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”.

Industry observers note that millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—consumers as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.

“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield remarked in a press release.

Industry observers note that states alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.

Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”.

According to recent reports, “Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.

Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the tech giant has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety noted that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues people who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.

“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety noted. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”.

However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises customers how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.

Industry observers note that nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled Upcoming York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok consumers, states alleged.

Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”.

Recent findings suggest that in its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”.

Recent findings suggest that “Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”.

It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”.

As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.

“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.

Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users.

“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.

In a recent development, although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It mentioned that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.

It has been revealed that “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones remarked. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this tech giant accountable.”.

Breaking: Introducing OpenAI

📅 11 Dec 2015 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that openAI is a non-profit artificial intelligence research manufacturer.
  • We believe AI should be an extension of individual human wills and, in the spirit of liberty, as broadly and evenly distributed as possible.
  • Industry observers note that artificial intelligence has always been a surprising field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that openAI is a non-profit artificial intelligence research manufacturer. Our goal is to advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return. Since our research is free from financial obligations, we can better focus on a positive human impact.

We believe AI should be an extension of individual human wills and, in the spirit of liberty, as broadly and evenly distributed as possible. The outcome of this venture is uncertain and the work is difficult, but we believe the goal and the structure are right. We hope this is what matters most to the best in the field.

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence has always been a surprising field. In the early days, people thought that solving certain tasks (such as chess) would lead us to discover human-level intelligence algorithms. However, the solution to each task turned out to be much less general than people were hoping (such as doing a search over a huge number of moves).

Industry observers note that the past few years have held another flavor of surprise. An AI technique explored for decades, deep learning, started achieving state-of-the-art results in a wide variety of problem domains. In deep learning, rather than hand-code a upcoming algorithm for each problem, you design architectures that can twist themselves into a wide range of algorithms based on the data you feed them.

This approach has yielded outstanding results on pattern recognition problems, such as recognizing objects in images, machine translation, and speech recognition. But we’ve also started to see what it might be like for computers to be creative⁠(opens in a latest window), to dream⁠(opens in a new window), and to experience the world⁠(opens in a new window).

AI systems today have impressive but narrow capabilities. It seems that we’ll keep whittling away at their constraints, and in the extreme case they will reach human performance on virtually every intellectual task. It’s hard to fathom how much human-level AI could benefit society, and it’s equally hard to imagine how much it could damage society if built or used incorrectly.

Because of AI’s surprising history, it’s hard to predict when human-level AI might come within reach. When it does, it’ll be important to have a leading research institution which can prioritize a good outcome for all over its own self-interest.

Recent findings suggest that we’re hoping to grow OpenAI into such an institution. As a non-profit, our aim is to build value for everyone rather than shareholders. Researchers will be strongly encouraged to publish their work, whether as papers, blog posts, or code, and our patents⁠ (if any) will be shared with the world. We’ll freely collaborate with others across many institutions and expect to work with companies to research and deploy fresh technologies.

According to recent reports, openAI’s research director is Ilya Sutskever⁠(opens in a new window), one of the world experts in machine learning. Our CTO is Greg Brockman⁠(opens in a new window), formerly the CTO of Stripe. The group’s other founding members are world-class research engineers and scientists: Trevor Blackwell⁠(opens in a new window), Vicki Cheung⁠(opens in a new window), Andrej Karpathy⁠(opens in a new window), Durk Kingma⁠(opens in a new window), John Schulman⁠(opens in a new window), Pamela Vagata⁠(opens in a new window), and Wojciech Zaremba⁠(opens in a new window). Pieter Abbeel, Yoshua Bengio, Alan Kay, Sergey Levine, and Vishal Sikka are advisors to the group. OpenAI’s co-chairs are Sam Altman and Elon Musk.

In a recent development, sam, Greg, Elon, Reid Hoffman, Jessica Livingston, Peter Thiel, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Infosys, and YC Research⁠(opens in a latest window) are donating to support OpenAI. In total, these funders have committed $1 billion, although we expect to only spend a tiny fraction of this in the next few years.

You can follow us on Twitter at @OpenAI⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

#28045. Weight normalization: A simple reparameterization to accelerate training of deep neural networks

📅 25 Feb 2016 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (167 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Weight normalization: A simple reparameterization to accelerate training of deep neural networks

📅 25 Feb 2016 | ⏱️ 1 min read (167 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We present weight normalization: a reparameterization of the weight vectors in a neural network that decouples the length of those weight vectors from their direction. By reparameterizing the weights in this way we improve the conditioning of the optimization problem and we speed up convergence of stochastic gradient descent. Our reparameterization is inspired by batch normalization but does not introduce any dependencies between the examples in a minibatch. This means that our method can also be applied successfully to recurrent models such as LSTMs and to noise-sensitive applications such as deep reinforcement learning or generative models, for which batch normalization is less well suited. Although our method is much simpler, it still provides much of the speed-up of full batch normalization. In addition, the computational overhead of our method is lower, permitting more optimization steps to be taken in the same amount of time. We demonstrate the usefulness of our method on applications in supervised image recognition, generative modelling, and deep reinforcement learning.

According to recent reports, pieter Abbeel. Pieter⁠(opens in a fresh window) is a professor at UC Berkeley specializing in making robots learn. He’s been giving us advice since before OpenAI was born, and now he’s taking a leave from Berkeley to work with us full-time. Pieter and his lab members have been responsible for some of the most striking advances in robot learning⁠(opens in a new window) and deep reinforcement learning (RL)⁠(opens in a new window) in recent years. Together, we will explore ways to combine unsupervised learning with RL, which we believe could address fundamental limitations in today’s RL algorithms.

According to recent reports, shivon Zilis. Shivon⁠(opens in a new window) is a partner at Bloomberg Beta⁠(opens in a new window) focusing on machine intelligence. She has an extremely broad view of how the space is evolving (and has⁠(opens in a new window) written⁠(opens in a new window) extensively⁠(opens in a new window) on the landscape). We’ve been going to her for advice for the past few months, and now she’s becoming an official advisor to OpenAI.

We could not be more excited to work with both. Welcome Pieter and Shivon!

#28042. OpenAI Gym Beta

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

OpenAI Gym Beta

📅 27 Apr 2016 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re releasing the public beta of OpenAI Gym, a toolkit for developing and comparing reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms.
  • OpenAI Gym is compatible with algorithms written in any framework, such as Tensorflow⁠(opens in a new window) and Theano⁠(opens in a new window).
  • If you’d like to dive in right away, you can work through our tutorial⁠(opens in a upcoming window).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’re releasing the public beta of OpenAI Gym, a toolkit for developing and comparing reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. It consists of a growing suite of environments (from simulated robots to Atari games), and a site for comparing and reproducing results.

OpenAI Gym is compatible with algorithms written in any framework, such as Tensorflow⁠(opens in a new window) and Theano⁠(opens in a new window). The environments are written in Python, but we’ll soon make them easy to use from any language. We originally built OpenAI Gym as a tool to accelerate our own RL research. We hope it will be just as useful for the broader community.

If you’d like to dive in right away, you can work through our tutorial⁠(opens in a upcoming window). You can also help out while learning by reproducing a result⁠(opens in a new window).

Reinforcement learning (RL) is the subfield of machine learning concerned with decision making and motor control. It studies how an agent can learn how to achieve goals in a complex, uncertain environment. It’s exciting for two reasons:.

Recent findings suggest that RL is very general, encompassing all problems that involve making a sequence of decisions: for example, controlling a robot’s motors so that it’s able to run⁠(opens in a new window) and jump⁠(opens in a new window), making business decisions like pricing and inventory management, or playing video games⁠(opens in a new window) and board games⁠(opens in a new window). RL can even be applied to supervised learning problems with sequential⁠(opens in a new window) or⁠(opens in a new window) structured⁠(opens in a new window) outputs.

RL algorithms have started to achieve good results in many difficult environments. RL has a long history, but until recent advances in deep learning, it required lots of problem-specific engineering. DeepMind’s Atari results⁠(opens in a new window), BRETT⁠(opens in a new window) from Pieter Abbeel’s⁠ group, and AlphaGo⁠(opens in a new window) all used deep RL algorithms which did not make too many assumptions about their environment, and thus can be applied in other settings.

However, RL research is also slowed down by two factors:.

It has been revealed that the need for better benchmarks. In supervised learning, progress has been driven by large labeled datasets like ImageNet⁠(opens in a new window). In RL, the closest equivalent would be a large and diverse collection of environments. However, the existing open-source collections of RL environments don’t have enough variety, and they are often difficult to even set up and use.

According to recent reports, lack of standardization of environments used in publications. Subtle differences in the problem definition, such as the reward function or the set of actions, can drastically alter a task’s difficulty. This issue makes it difficult to reproduce published research and compare results from different papers.

OpenAI Gym is an attempt to fix both problems.

Industry observers note that openAI Gym provides a diverse suite of environments that range from easy to difficult and involve many different kinds of data. We’re starting out with the following collections:.

According to recent reports, classic control⁠(opens in a fresh window) and toy text⁠(opens in a new window): complete small-scale tasks, mostly from the RL literature. They’re here to get you started.

Sources indicate that algorithmic⁠(opens in a newly introduced window): perform computations such as adding multi-digit numbers and reversing sequences. One might object that these tasks are easy for a computer. The challenge is to learn these algorithms purely from examples. These tasks have the nice property that it’s easy to vary the difficulty by varying the sequence length.

Atari⁠(opens in a upcoming window): play classic Atari games. We’ve integrated the Arcade Learning Environment⁠(opens in a new window) (which has had a big impact on reinforcement learning research) in an easy-to-install⁠(opens in a new window) form.

Board games⁠(opens in a new window): play Go on 9x9 and 19x19 boards. Two-player games are fundamentally different than the other settings we’ve included, because there is an adversary playing against you. In our initial release, there is a fixed opponent provided by Pachi⁠(opens in a new window), and we may add other opponents later (patches welcome!). We’ll also likely expand OpenAI Gym to have first-class support for multi-player games.

2D and 3D robots⁠(opens in a new window): control a robot in simulation. These tasks use the MuJoCo⁠(opens in a new window) physics engine, which was designed for fast and accurate robot simulation. Included are some environments from a recent benchmark⁠(opens in a new window) by UC Berkeley researchers (who incidentally will be joining us⁠ this summer). MuJoCo is proprietary software, but offers free trial⁠(opens in a new window) licenses.

Recent findings suggest that over time, we blueprint to greatly expand this collection of environments. Contributions from the community are more than welcome.

Recent findings suggest that each environment has a version number (such as Hopper-v0⁠(opens in a newly introduced window)). If we need to change an environment, we’ll bump the version number, defining an entirely new task. This ensures that results on a particular environment are always comparable.

We’ve made it easy to upload results⁠(opens in a fresh window) to OpenAI Gym. However, we’ve opted not to create traditional leaderboards. What matters for research isn’t your score (it’s possible to overfit or hand-craft solutions to particular tasks), but instead the generality of your technique.

We’re starting out by maintaining a curated list⁠(opens in a fresh window) of contributions that say something interesting about algorithmic capabilities. Long-term, we want this curation to be a community effort rather than something owned by us. We’ll necessarily have to figure out the details over time, and we’d would love your help⁠(opens in a new window) in doing so.

Industry observers note that we want OpenAI Gym to be a community effort from the beginning. We’ve starting working with partners to put together resources around OpenAI Gym:.

NVIDIA⁠(opens in a upcoming window): technical Q&A⁠(opens in a new window) with John.

Nervana⁠(opens in a new window): implementation of a DQN OpenAI Gym agent⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that amazon Web Services (AWS)⁠(opens in a new window): $250 credit vouchers for select OpenAI Gym owners. If you have an evaluation demonstrating the promise of your algorithm and are resource-constrained from scaling it up, ping us⁠ for a voucher. (While supplies last!).

According to recent reports, during the public beta, we’re looking for feedback on how to make this into an even better tool for research. If you’d like to help, you can try your hand at improving the state-of-the-art on each environment, reproducing other people’s results, or even implementing your own environments. Also please join us in the community chat⁠(opens in a upcoming window)!

#28040. Breaking: Adversarial training methods for semi-supervised text classification

📅 25 May 2016 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (140 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Adversarial training methods for semi-supervised text classification

📅 25 May 2016 | ⏱️ 1 min read (140 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Adversarial training provides a means of regularizing supervised learning algorithms while virtual adversarial training is able to extend supervised learning algorithms to the semi-supervised setting. However, both methods require making small perturbations to numerous entries of the input vector, which is inappropriate for sparse high-dimensional inputs such as one-hot word representations. We extend adversarial and virtual adversarial training to the text domain by applying perturbations to the word embeddings in a recurrent neural network rather than to the original input itself. The proposed method achieves state of the art results on multiple benchmark semi-supervised and purely supervised tasks. We provide visualizations and analysis showing that the learned word embeddings have improved in quality and that while training, the model is less prone to overfitting. Code is available at this https URL⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

Generative models

📅 16 Jun 2016 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this post describes four projects that share a common theme of enhancing or using generative models, a branch of unsupervised learning techniques in machine learning.
  • One of our core aspirations at OpenAI is to develop algorithms and techniques that endow computers with an understanding of our world.
  • It’s easy to forget just how much you know about the world: you understand that it is made up of 3D environments, objects that move, collide, interact; people who walk, talk, and think; animals who graze, fly, run, or bark; monitors that display information encoded in language about the weather, who won a basketball game, or what happened in 1970.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Illustration: Ludwig Pettersson.

Industry observers note that this post describes four projects that share a common theme of enhancing or using generative models, a branch of unsupervised learning techniques in machine learning. In addition to describing our work, this post will tell you a bit more about generative models: what they are, why they are key, and where they might be going.

One of our core aspirations at OpenAI is to develop algorithms and techniques that endow computers with an understanding of our world.

It’s easy to forget just how much you know about the world: you understand that it is made up of 3D environments, objects that move, collide, interact; people who walk, talk, and think; animals who graze, fly, run, or bark; monitors that display information encoded in language about the weather, who won a basketball game, or what happened in 1970.

This tremendous amount of information is out there and to a large extent easily accessible—either in the physical world of atoms or the digital world of bits. The only tricky part is to develop models and algorithms that can analyze and understand this treasure trove of data.

Generative models are one of the most promising approaches towards this goal. To train a generative model we first collect a large amount of data in some domain (e.g., think millions of images, sentences, or sounds, etc.) and then train a model to generate data like it. The intuition behind this approach follows a famous quote from Richard Feynman⁠(opens in a new window):.

The trick is that the neural networks we use as generative models have a number of parameters significantly smaller than the amount of data we train them on, so the models are forced to discover and efficiently internalize the essence of the data in order to generate it.

Recent findings suggest that generative models have many short-term applications⁠. But in the long run, they hold the potential to automatically learn the natural features of a dataset, whether categories or dimensions or something else entirely.

Let’s make this more concrete with an example. Suppose we have some large collection of images, such as the 1.2 million images in the ImageNet⁠(opens in a upcoming window) dataset (but keep in mind that this could eventually be a large collection of images or videos from the internet or robots). If we resize each image to have width and height of 256 (as is commonly done), our dataset is one large 1,200,000x256x256x3 (about 200GB) block of pixels. Here are a few example images from this dataset:.

According to recent reports, these images are examples of what our visual world looks like and we refer to these as “samples from the true data distribution”. We now construct our generative model which we would like to train to generate images like this from scratch. Concretely, a generative model in this case could be one large neural network that outputs images and we refer to these as “samples from the model”.

According to recent reports, one such recent model is the DCGAN network⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) from Radford et al. (shown below). This network takes as input 100 random numbers drawn from a uniform distribution⁠(opens in a new window) (we refer to these as a code, or latent variables, in red) and outputs an image (in this case 64x64x3 images on the right, in green). As the code is changed incrementally, the generated images⁠(opens in a new window) do too—this shows the model has learned features to describe how the world looks, rather than just memorizing some examples.

The network (in yellow) is made up of standard convolutional neural network⁠(opens in a new window) components, such as deconvolutional layers⁠(opens in a new window) (reverse of convolutional layers), fully connected layers⁠(opens in a new window), etc.:.

In a recent development, DCGAN is initialized with random weights, so a random code plugged into the network would generate a completely random image. However, as you might imagine, the network has millions of parameters that we can tweak, and the goal is to find a setting of these parameters that makes samples generated from random codes look like the training data. Or to put it another way, we want the model distribution to match the true data distribution in the space of images.

Suppose that we used a newly-initialized network to generate 200 images, each time starting with a different random code. The question is: how should we adjust the network’s parameters to encourage it to produce slightly more believable samples in the future? Notice that we’re not in a simple supervised setting and don’t have any explicit desired targets for our 200 generated images; we merely want them to look real. One clever approach around this problem is to follow the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)⁠(opens in a latest window) approach. Here we introduce a second discriminator network (usually a standard convolutional neural network) that tries to classify if an input image is real or generated. For instance, we could feed the 200 generated images and 200 real images into the discriminator and train it as a standard classifier to distinguish between the two sources. But in addition to that—and here’s the trick—we can also backpropagate⁠(opens in a new window) through both the discriminator and the generator to find how we should change the generator’s parameters to make its 200 samples slightly more confusing for the discriminator. These two networks are therefore locked in a battle: the discriminator is trying to distinguish real images from fake images and the generator is trying to create images that make the discriminator think they are real. In the end, the generator network is outputting images that are indistinguishable from real images for the discriminator.

According to recent reports, there are a few other approaches to matching these distributions which we will discuss briefly below. But before we get there below are two animations that show samples from a generative model to give you a visual sense for the training process.In both cases the samples from the generator start out noisy and chaotic, and over time converge to have more plausible image statistics:.

VAE learning to generate images (log time).

GAN learning to generate images (linear time).

This is exciting—these neural networks are learning what the visual world looks like! These models usually have only about 100 million parameters, so a network trained on ImageNet has to (lossily) compress⁠(opens in a new window) 200GB of pixel data into 100MB of weights. This incentivizes it to discover the most salient features of the data: for example, it will likely learn that pixels nearby are likely to have the same color, or that the world is made up of horizontal or vertical edges, or blobs of different colors. Eventually, the model may discover many more complex regularities: that there are certain types of backgrounds, objects, textures, that they occur in certain likely arrangements, or that they transform in certain ways over time in videos, etc.

Mathematically, we think about a dataset of examples x1,…,xn x_1, \ldots, x_n x1​,…,xn​ as samples from a true data distribution  p(x) p(x)  p(x). In the example image below, the blue region shows the part of the image space that, with a high probability (over some threshold) contains real images, and black dots indicate our data points (each is one image in our dataset). Now, our model also describes a distribution p^θ(x) \hat{p}_{\theta}(x) p^​θ​(x) (green) that is defined implicitly by taking points from a unit Gaussian distribution⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) (red) and mapping them through a (deterministic) neural network—our generative model (yellow). Our network is a function with parameters θ \theta θ, and tweaking these parameters will tweak the generated distribution of images. Our goal then is to find parameters θ \theta θ that produce a distribution that closely matches the true data distribution (for example, by having a small KL divergence⁠(opens in a new window) loss⁠(opens in a new window)). Therefore, you can imagine the green distribution starting out random and then the training process iteratively changing the parameters θ \theta θ to stretch and squeeze it to better match the blue distribution.

Most generative models have this basic setup, but differ in the details. Here are three popular examples of generative model approaches to give you a sense of the variation:.

Sources indicate that generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)⁠(opens in a fresh window), which we already discussed above, pose the training process as a game between two separate networks: a generator network (as seen above) and a second discriminative network that tries to classify samples as either coming from the true distribution  p(x) p(x)  p(x) or the model distribution p^(x) \hat{p}(x) p^​(x). Every time the discriminator notices a difference between the two distributions the generator adjusts its parameters slightly to make it go away, until at the end (in theory) the generator exactly reproduces the true data distribution and the discriminator is guessing at random, unable to find a difference.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)⁠(opens in a fresh window) allow us to formalize this problem in the framework of probabilistic graphical models⁠(opens in a new window) where we are maximizing a lower bound⁠(opens in a new window) on the log likelihood of the data.

In a recent development, autoregressive models such as PixelRNN⁠(opens in a new window) instead train a network that models the conditional distribution of every individual pixel given previous pixels (to the left and to the top). This is similar to plugging the pixels of the image into a char-rnn⁠(opens in a new window), but the RNNs run both horizontally and vertically over the image instead of just a 1D sequence of characters.

All of these approaches have their pros and cons. For example, Variational Autoencoders allow us to perform both learning and efficient Bayesian inference in sophisticated probabilistic graphical models with latent variables (e.g. see DRAW⁠(opens in a fresh window), or Attend Infer Repeat⁠(opens in a new window) for hints of recent relatively complex models). However, their generated samples tend to be slightly blurry. GANs currently generate the sharpest images but they are more difficult to optimize due to unstable training dynamics. PixelRNNs have a very simple and stable training process (softmax loss⁠(opens in a new window)) and currently give the best log likelihoods (that is, plausibility of the generated data). However, they are relatively inefficient during sampling and don’t easily provide simple low-dimensional codes for images. All of these models are active areas of research and we are eager to see how they develop in the future!

In a recent development, we’re quite excited about generative models at OpenAI, and have just released four projects that advance the state of the art. For each of these contributions we are also releasing a technical report and source code.

It has been revealed that improving GANs⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) (code⁠(opens in a new window)). First, as mentioned above GANs are a very promising family of generative models because, unlike other methods, they produce very clean and sharp images and learn codes that contain valuable information about these textures. However, GANs are formulated as a game between two networks and it is key (and tricky!) to keep them in balance: for example, they can oscillate between solutions, or the generator has a tendency to collapse. In this work, Tim Salimans, Ian Goodfellow, Wojciech Zaremba and colleagues have introduced a few new techniques for making GAN training more stable. These techniques allow us to scale up GANs and obtain nice 128x128 ImageNet samples:.

Our CIFAR-10⁠(opens in a latest window) samples also look very sharp - Amazon Mechanical Turk workers can distinguish our samples from real data with an error rate of 21.3% (50% would be random guessing):.

In addition to generating pretty pictures, we introduce an approach for semi-supervised learning⁠(opens in a new window) with GANs that involves the discriminator producing an additional output indicating the label of the input. This approach allows us to obtain state of the art results on MNIST⁠(opens in a new window), SVHN⁠(opens in a new window), and CIFAR-10 in settings with very few labeled examples⁠(opens in a new window). On MNIST, for example, we achieve 99.14% accuracy with only 10 labeled examples per class with a fully connected neural network—a result that’s very close to the best known results with fully supervised approaches using all 60,000 labeled examples. This is very promising because labeled examples can be quite expensive to obtain in practice.

Generative Adversarial Networks are a relatively new model (introduced only two years ago) and we expect to see more rapid progress in further improving the stability of these models during training.

Improving VAEs⁠(opens in a new window) (code⁠(opens in a new window)). In this work Durk Kingma and Tim Salimans introduce a flexible and computationally scalable method for improving the accuracy of variational inference⁠(opens in a new window). In particular, most VAEs have so far been trained using crude approximate posteriors⁠(opens in a new window), where every latent variable is independent. Recent extensions⁠(opens in a new window) have addressed this problem by conditioning each latent variable on the others before it in a chain, but this is computationally inefficient due to the introduced sequential dependencies. The core contribution of this work, termed inverse autoregressive flow (IAF), is a new approach that, unlike previous work, allows us to parallelize the computation of rich approximate posteriors, and make them almost arbitrarily flexible.

Recent findings suggest that we show some example 32x32 image samples from the model in the image below, on the right. On the left are earlier samples from the DRAW⁠(opens in a upcoming window) model for comparison (vanilla VAE samples would look even worse and more blurry). The DRAW model was published only one year ago, highlighting again the rapid progress being made in training generative models.

Generated from a VAE trained with IAF.

Industry observers note that infoGAN⁠(opens in a new window) (code⁠(opens in a new window)). Peter Chen and colleagues introduce InfoGAN—an extension of GAN that learns disentangled and interpretable representations for images. A regular GAN achieves the objective of reproducing the data distribution in the model, but the layout and organization of the code space is underspecified—there are many possible solutions to mapping the unit Gaussian to images and the one we end up with might be intricate and highly entangled. The InfoGAN imposes additional structure on this space by adding new objectives that involve maximizing the mutual information⁠(opens in a new window) between small subsets of the representation variables and the observation. This approach provides quite remarkable results. For example, in the images of 3D faces below we vary one continuous dimension of the code, keeping all others fixed. It’s clear from the five provided examples (along each row) that the resulting dimensions in the code capture interpretable dimensions, and that the model has perhaps understood that there are camera angles, facial variations, etc., without having been told that these features exist and are crucial:.

We also note that nice, disentangled representations have been achieved before (such as with DC-IGN⁠(opens in a fresh window) by Kulkarni et al.), but these approaches rely on additional supervision, while our approach is entirely unsupervised.

The next two recent projects are in a reinforcement learning⁠(opens in a new window) (RL) setting (another area of focus⁠ at OpenAI), but they both involve a generative model component.

Industry observers note that curiosity-driven Exploration in Deep Reinforcement Learning via Bayesian Neural Networks⁠(opens in a new window) (code⁠(opens in a new window)). Efficient exploration in high-dimensional and continuous spaces is presently an unsolved challenge in reinforcement learning. Without effective exploration methods our agents thrash around⁠(opens in a new window) until they randomly stumble into rewarding situations. This is sufficient in many simple toy tasks but inadequate if we wish to apply these algorithms to complex settings with high-dimensional action spaces, as is common in robotics. In this paper, Rein Houthooft and colleagues propose VIME, a practical approach to exploration using uncertainty on generative models. VIME makes the agent self-motivated; it actively seeks out surprising state-actions. We show that VIME can improve a range of policy search⁠(opens in a new window) methods and makes significant progress on more realistic tasks with sparse rewards (e.g. scenarios in which the agent has to learn locomotion primitives without any guidance).

Policy trained with naive exploration.

In a recent development, finally, we would like to include a bonus fifth project: Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning⁠(opens in a latest window) (code⁠(opens in a new window)), in which Jonathan Ho and colleagues present a new approach for imitation learning. Jonathan Ho is joining us at OpenAI as a summer intern. He did most of this work at Stanford but we include it here as a related and highly creative application of GANs to RL. The standard reinforcement learning setting usually requires one to design a reward function that describes the desired behavior of the agent. However, in practice this can sometimes involve expensive trial-and-error process to get the details right. In contrast, in imitation learning the agent learns from example demonstrations (for example provided by teleoperation in robotics), eliminating the need to design a reward function.

Popular imitation approaches involve a two-stage pipeline: first learning a reward function, then running RL on that reward. Such a pipeline can be slow, and because it’s indirect, it is hard to guarantee that the resulting policy works well. This work indicates how one can directly extract policies from data via a connection to GANs. As a result, this approach can be used to learn policies from expert demonstrations (without rewards) on hard OpenAI Gym⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) environments, such as Ant⁠(opens in a new window) and Humanoid⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that generative models are a rapidly advancing area of research. As we continue to advance these models and scale up the training and the datasets, we can expect to eventually generate samples that depict entirely plausible images or videos. This may by itself find use in multiple applications, such as on-demand generated art, or Photoshop++ commands such as “make my smile wider”. Additional presently known applications include image denoising⁠(opens in a fresh window), inpainting⁠(opens in a new window), super-resolution⁠(opens in a new window), structured prediction⁠(opens in a new window), exploration⁠(opens in a new window) in reinforcement learning, and neural network pretraining⁠(opens in a new window) in cases where labeled data is expensive.

However, the deeper promise of this work is that, in the process of training generative models, we will endow the computer with an understanding of the world and what it is made up of.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI’s mission is to build safe AI, and ensure AI’s benefits are as widely and evenly distributed as possible.
  • In a recent development, we’re trying to build AI as part of a larger community, and we want to share our plans and capabilities along the way.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI’s mission is to build safe AI, and ensure AI’s benefits are as widely and evenly distributed as possible.

In a recent development, we’re trying to build AI as part of a larger community, and we want to share our plans and capabilities along the way. We’re also working to solidify our organization’s governance structure and will share our thoughts on that later this year.

In a recent development, defining a metric for intelligence is tricky, but we need one to measure our progress and focus our research. We’re thus building a living metric which measures how well an agent can achieve its user’s intended goal in a wide range of environments.

In a recent development, the metric will consist of a variety of OpenAI Gym⁠(opens in a upcoming window) environments with a unified action and observation space⁠(opens in a new window) (so a single agent can run across all of them), including games, robotics, and language-based tasks. Our implementation will evolve over time, and we’ll keep the community updated along the way.

A significant fraction of our research bandwidth is being spent on fundamental research. We’ll always be developing and testing new ideas, especially those that don’t fit neatly into our current worldview. This is important—our current ideas will not be enough to achieve our long-term goal.

It has been revealed that we’ve also formed teams around specific projects. The intention isn’t just to solve these problems, but to develop general learning algorithms in the process. These algorithms will, in turn, help us build agents that are more capable according to our metric. These projects are:.

We’re working to enable a physical robot (off-the-shelf; not manufactured by OpenAI) to perform basic housework. There are existing⁠(opens in a new window) techniques⁠(opens in a new window) for specific tasks, but we believe that learning algorithms can eventually be made reliable⁠(opens in a new window) enough⁠(opens in a new window) to create a general-purpose robot. More generally, robotics is a good testbed for many challenges in AI.

We proposal to build an agent that can perform a complex task specified by language, and ask for clarification about the task if it’s ambiguous. Today, there are promising algorithms for supervised language tasks such as question⁠(opens in a fresh window) answering⁠(opens in a new window), syntactic⁠(opens in a new window) parsing⁠(opens in a new window) and machine⁠(opens in a new window) translation⁠(opens in a new window) but there aren’t any for more advanced linguistic goals, such as the ability to carry a conversation, the ability to fully understand a document, and the ability to follow complex instructions in natural language. We expect to develop new learning algorithms and paradigms to tackle these problems.

We aim to train an agent capable enough to solve any game in our initial metric. Games are virtual mini-worlds that are very diverse, and learning to play games quickly and well will require significant advances in generative models⁠ and reinforcement learning⁠(opens in a latest window). (We are inspired by the pioneering work of DeepMind⁠(opens in a new window), who have produced impressive⁠(opens in a new window) results⁠(opens in a new window) in this area in the past few years.).

Our projects and fundamental research all have shared cores, so progress on any is likely to benefit the others. Each captures a different aspect of goal-solving, and was chosen for its potential to significantly move our metric.

In a recent development, we’re just getting started on these projects, and the details may change as we gain additional data. We also expect to add upcoming projects over time.
